name: Swedish (Central Standard)
family: Indo-European, Germanic, North Germanic, East Scandinavian
variety: Central Standard Swedish, the educated speech of Stockholm and the Mälaren region, the variety of the IPA illustration (Engstrand 1990)
sources: Engstrand, Olle (1990). Swedish. Journal of the International Phonetic Association 20(1), 42-44. Reprinted in the Handbook of the International Phonetic Association (1999), Cambridge University Press.
Riad, Tomas (2014). The Phonology of Swedish. Oxford University Press.
Bruce, Gösta (1977). Swedish Word Accents in Sentence Perspective. Lund: Gleerup.
Bruce, Gösta and Gårding, Eva (1978). A prosodic typology for Swedish dialects. In Gårding, Bruce and Bannert (eds.), Nordic Prosody. Lund University.
Elert, Claes-Christian (1964). Phonologic Studies of Quantity in Swedish. Stockholm: Almqvist and Wiksell.
Lindblad, Per (1980). Svenskans sje- och tje-ljud i ett allmänfonetiskt perspektiv. Lund: Gleerup.
Helgason, Pétur and Ringen, Catherine (2008). Voicing and aspiration in Swedish stops. Journal of Phonetics 36, 607-628.
Kuronen, Mikko (2001). Acoustic character of vowel pronunciation in Sweden-Swedish and Finland-Swedish. Lund University, Department of Linguistics, Working Papers 49, 94-97.
Fant, Gunnar; Henningsson, Gunnar; Stålhammar, Ulf (1969). Formant frequencies of Swedish vowels. Speech Transmission Laboratory Quarterly Progress and Status Report 10(4), 26-31.
contrasts: two word accents on stressed syllables of words with at least one following syllable: accent 1 anden 'the duck' versus accent 2 anden 'the spirit', tomten 'the plot' versus 'the gnome', buren 'the cage' versus 'carried', stegen 'the steps' versus 'the ladder'
complementary quantity in stressed syllables: long vowel plus short consonant versus short vowel plus long consonant (glas [ɡlɑːs] versus glass [ɡlasː], vit versus vitt, ful versus full)
long and short vowels differ in quality as well as length, most of all /ɑː/ versus /a/ and /ʉː/ versus /ɵ/
three close rounded vowels /yː ʉː uː/ with different kinds of lip rounding (ny, nu, bo)
three voiceless sibilant-like fricatives: /s/, the tj-sound /ɕ/ (tjugo, kör) and the sj-sound /ɧ/ (sju, sked, stjärna)
dental /t d n s l/ versus retroflex [ʈ ɖ ɳ ʂ ɭ] (kort, bord, barn, fors, karl)
allophony: /r/ plus a following /t d n s l/ fuse to retroflex [ʈ ɖ ɳ ʂ ɭ], inside words and across word boundaries (kort [kɔʈː], bord [buːɖ], barn [bɑːɳ], fors [fɔʂː], för stor [fœˈʂʈuːr], har du); the retroflexion spreads through a cluster (först [fœʂʈ])
/ɛː ɛ/ are lowered to [æː æ] and /øː œ/ to [œː œ] before /r/ and the retroflexes (här [hæːr], järn [jæːɳ], kör [ɕœːr], dörr)
long close vowels end in a narrowing with friction ([iːʝ], [yː] and [ʉː] with a labial offglide); long mid vowels /eː øː oː/ often end in a centring glide; short vowels are steady
the sj-sound /ɧ/ is a rounded velar or labiodental-velar fricative before stressed vowels for most central speakers, and a retroflex-like [ʂ] at the end of a syllable and for some speakers everywhere
/r/ is seldom a full trill: it is a tap, a fricative or an approximant, and may be a trill in emphatic speech

/p t k/ are aspirated before a stressed vowel, unaspirated after /s/, and often preaspirated after a short stressed vowel (tack, vitt); /b d ɡ/ are voiced, with prevoicing at the start of an utterance
short /e/ and /ɛ/ have merged in the central standard
unstressed e is a mid central vowel in endings (flickan, bilen)
/ŋ/ occurs for ng and for g before n (regn [rɛŋn], lång)
/k ɡ sk/ before stressed front vowels are /ɕ j ɧ/ in native words (kör, göra, sked), with exceptions among loans and some words (kö [køː], kille)
/j/ is a palatal approximant, often with friction; /l/ is clear in all positions
phonotactics: a stressed syllable is heavy: it has a long vowel, or a short vowel followed by a long consonant or a cluster
unstressed syllables have short vowels and short consonants
onset clusters of up to three consonants, the first being /s/ (spr, str, skr, spl)
retroflex consonants do not begin words in isolation, and /ŋ/ never begins a word
accent 2 needs at least one syllable after the stressed one; monosyllables and words with final stress have accent 1

stress.rule: Native words stress the first syllable of the stem, the prefixes be- and för- are unstressed, compounds have main stress on the first member and a secondary stress on the last, and loans often stress the last or second-last syllable (banan, station, universitet).
stress.cues: quantity (the long vowel or long consonant of the stressed syllable), the tonal gesture of the word accent, and intensity

rhythm.vowel_reduction: moderate: unstressed vowels are short and unstressed e is centralised, but a, i, o, u keep their quality in endings
rhythm.notes: I know of no nPVI value for Swedish in the studies I can cite.

length.notes: Length is complementary in stressed syllables. Kuronen (2001) found short vowels to be on average 67 per cent as long as their long partners in Central Standard Swedish (Nyköping speakers). The consonant after a short stressed vowel is long; Elert (1964) is the classic study.

intonation.declarative: every stressed word has the fall of its word accent; the focused word adds a rise to a high tone after that fall (the sentence accent); after the focus the pitch is low and the accents are compressed, and the statement ends in a fall to a low boundary
intonation.yes_no_question: the verb-first word order marks the question; the pitch is higher overall, the range is wider and the final fall is smaller; a final rise is possible but not required
intonation.wh_question: as in statements, with the focus often on the question word or on a later word, and a final fall
intonation.continuation: the rise of the sentence accent is left high at the end of the phrase, without a fall to the bottom of the range
intonation.accent_shape: accent 1 is HL*: the fall comes early, so that the stressed syllable is low; accent 2 is H*L: the stressed syllable starts high and the fall takes place within it; in both, focus adds a high tone after the fall, in accent 2 on the syllable after the stressed one, in compounds on the last stressed member
intonation.notes: Analysis of Bruce (1977) for Stockholm. The timing difference between the two accent falls is the constant cue; the second peak of accent 2 belongs to the sentence accent and is absent out of focus. Dialects differ in timing and in the number of peaks (Bruce and Gårding 1978).

inventory.name: accent 1 (acute)
inventory.description: the accent fall is completed before or at the start of the stressed syllable, which is therefore low; in focus a rise to high follows, late in the stressed syllable or in the next one, and the word said alone ends in a fall: one peak

inventory.name: accent 2 (grave)
inventory.description: the stressed syllable starts high and falls; in focus a second rise to high follows on the next syllable (in compounds on the last stressed member), and the word said alone ends in a fall: two peaks

sandhi: out of focus only the word accent fall remains: accent 1 is low on the stressed syllable after a high on the syllable before, accent 2 is high falling on the stressed syllable
compounds take accent 2 in Central Standard Swedish whatever the accents of their parts
the definite article does not change the accent of the stem: and-en from the monosyllable and keeps accent 1, ande-n from ande keeps accent 2
accents after the focus are compressed in range
tone.neutral_tone: unstressed syllables have no accent of their own; they carry the end of the accent fall, the focal rise, or the low stretch up to the next accent
tone.notes: The Chao numerals are a schematic rendering of the citation form (with focus and final fall) of a word of two syllables with initial stress, not measured values. eSpeak NG has no tone phonemes for Swedish, so the espeak field is empty.

phonation: aspiration and preaspiration of /p t k/; no contrastive voice quality

problems: the word accents are not marked anywhere: the phoneme table has no tone phonemes and the dictionary has no accent marks, so both words anden, tomten, buren and stegen sound the same; the Swedish tunes (sv_s, sv_c, sv_q, sv_e) only shape the intonation of the clause
complementary quantity is incomplete: the consonant after a short stressed vowel is mostly left short (matt [mat], tack [tak], full [fɵl], glass [ɡlas]); only some spelling rules add length (flickan)

retroflexion is unreliable for rt: kort is [kɔrt], hjärta and skjorta lose the r and keep a dental [t], värld is [vɛːrd]; there is no retroflexion across word boundaries (för stor, har du, Anders sover)
the lowering before r is missing: här, ära have [ɛː], kör and björn have [øː], dörr has [œ] of normal height; järn has a short vowel
rule errors: kö comes out with the tj-sound, giraff with [j] and initial stress, station with [sj] instead of the sj-sound, regn with schwa, lång with a close [o], universitet with initial stress
stops have no preaspiration, and long vowels have no diphthongal offglides
questions are given the same tune whether they are yes-no or wh-questions
good: the sj-sound has its own phoneme with a recorded fricative, and the tj-sound is an alveolo-palatal [ɕ]
retroflex [ɖ ɳ ʂ ɭ] are produced from rd, rn, rs, rl inside words (bord, barn, fors, karl, först)
long and short vowels are separate phonemes that differ in quality and duration, including [ʉː] against [ɵ] and [ɑː] against [a]
the voice has its own tunes with a wide pitch range

notes: In the consonant list the retroflexes are the fused forms of /r/ plus a dental. In the vowel list [æ æː œː] are the lowered allophones before /r/. The diphthongs au and ɛu occur in loans (paus, Europa). I give no formant or voice onset time values because I cannot quote the published figures with confidence; Fant, Henningsson and Stålhammar (1969) and Helgason and Ringen (2008) are the sources to consult.
